output.title: Focus blocks come after the workflow decision
output.body:
Before you protect a focus block, decide what is actually stealing the focus.

For a small business owner, the useful question is not whether AI sounds smart. It is whether one recurring task keeps interrupting the day: repeated customer questions, invoice data entry, or lead follow-up. If the work changes every time, it is probably not the first thing to automate. If it shows a pattern, repeats weekly, and has a clear input and output, you have a workflow worth looking at.

That is the bounded decision Bareni starts with: identify one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and then decide whether it stays manual, gets shared with a hire, or is scoped for a pilot. That sequence is a normal operating practice, not a promise. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees. No spreadsheet heroics required; a plain week of notes usually tells you more than a clever guess.

The first move is simple: name the one task, time how often it interrupts your week, and check whether it really repeats before you protect the block. If it is a one-off, keep it manual and move on. If it is a pattern, you can decide what belongs in the workflow and what belongs in the calendar.
